questionnaire.title: Adult Kink & BDSM Preference Inventory
designNotes: Neutral self-assessment taxonomy for adults.
Fantasy appeal, experience, willingness, and boundaries are stored independently.
Hard limits stop descendant branches by default but never overwrite direct child answers.
Unanswered values are null/absent, never treated as neutral.
High-risk concepts are taxonomy labels only; the catalog contains no procedural instructions.
Question-specific detail profiles replace generic detail matrices in the prototype UI.
Concept perspectives are semantic (for example as_dominant/as_submissive) where give/receive would be misleading.
Detail questions expand inline after a positive/curious answer rather than requiring a Details button.
Directional acts are modeled as one concept with semantic perspectives where possible (for example Oral sex -> Giving / Receiving).
Emotional arousal is modeled independently from physical activities so the inventory can distinguish what someone likes doing from how they like feeling.
Partner gender, gender expression, anatomy, and body traits are modeled independently and can vary by activity.
The questionnaire avoids asking users to explain why a preference is erotic; it records observable preferences and lets interpretation emerge from the pattern.
Motivation is represented in the schema but is not directly questioned by default; future analysis may infer it from response patterns.
Body/anatomy compatibility is a separate optional follow-up family and never implies gender from anatomy or anatomy from gender.
Detailed categories are grouped into eight navigation domains; domains organize discovery without changing canonical answer ownership.
Every concept declares canonicalId, primaryCategory, relatedCategories, domain, and semanticTags; categoryIds remains a compatibility mirror.
A canonical concept may be shown in multiple related categories while all placements write to the same concept/perspective answer key.
Every concept has an explicit semanticType and questionModel template; semantic type controls which base question dimensions are meaningful.
Fantasy appeal, real-world desire, willingness/openness, experience, and boundaries are separate constructs and are stored independently.
Fantasy-only is a first-class willingness stance rather than a generic condition.
Impossible or purely imagined fantasy concepts do not ask physical-experience questions.
Body-part, material, and stimulus concepts use attraction/real-world-interest templates rather than activity-shaped experience questions.
Adaptive detail branches use explicit parent states; interested/open/unsure states expand by default, while not-interested and hard-limit states collapse without deleting saved details.
Fantasy-only parent states show fantasy-relevant detail fields while suppressing real-world implementation fields.
Collapsed adaptive branches can always be manually expanded; automatic branching assists navigation but does not block nuance.
Preference-matrix detail fields store each subtype independently as appealing, acceptable, conditional, not interested, or hard limit.
Distinct implements, body-part interests, materials, roles, emotions, and sexual activities remain canonical concepts when independent preference differences are meaningful.
Results aggregate scored perspectives into a concept-level value before category/domain aggregation, so concepts with more perspectives do not receive extra default weight.
Hard limits, category-wide boundaries, conditional states, not-interested states, and unanswered states are reported separately from preference averages.
Results keep fantasy appeal, real-world desire, experience, willingness, perspective, conditions, and boundaries as separate dimensions; qualitative labels are preferred over raw percentages.
General communication, stop/check-in, aftercare, marks, privacy, and partner-context preferences are stored in a separate negotiationPreferences profile and never folded into concept interest scores.
Plan 07 replaces generic risk severity labels with descriptive multi-domain risk metadata and high-level, non-procedural prompts tied to the actual concern domain.

psychological_context.text: Consider emotional boundaries, vulnerable topics, the intended tone, and what kind of check-in or aftercare would help this feel well negotiated.

consent_complexity_negotiation.label: Consent complexity
consent_complexity_negotiation.text: Prior negotiation and a clear, mutually understood way to pause, check in, or stop are especially important when consent may be harder to communicate in the moment.

privacy_handling.label: Privacy considerations
privacy_handling.text: Clarify who may see, know about, or retain information or media connected with this interest, including identification and sharing boundaries.

digital_media_handling.label: Digital security considerations
digital_media_handling.text: Discuss storage, screenshots, identification, account or device access, redistribution, and deletion expectations before creating or exchanging digital material.

reputational_exposure.label: Reputational / social considerations
reputational_exposure.text: Consider accidental disclosure, who might encounter the activity or records of it, and any social, family, or professional visibility boundaries.

financial_limits.label: Financial considerations
financial_limits.text: Set explicit financial limits and boundaries in advance, including what forms of spending or transfer are never on the table and how changes would be agreed.

riskMigration.rule: Legacy severity labels were not converted one-for-one. Each concept was reassigned zero or more descriptive concern domains using category, concept identity, and media/context semantics; no domain is a moral or psychometric severity score.
